`tidycreel` can now take a creel survey from a sampling calendar and raw field
tables through counts, interviews, catch, and lengths to rates, totals, section
and species results, and uncertainty estimates. The question driving the work
right now is no longer simply what the package can do. It is whether an analyst
can trust a result, understand how it was made, and give a colleague enough
information to check it.

Over the past few days, I have been working less on new functions and more on
the contracts around existing estimates: which interviews they use, which
estimator produced them, and when the package should stop instead of returning a
plausible but mismatched number. That can look quiet from outside the project.
Often the visible change is a number that does not move, a label that finally
matches the calculation, or an error that arrives before the result is reported.

That sounds obvious. It is also where creel analysis gets difficult.

A survey can have a reasonable sampling schedule, careful field staff, and a
well-organized set of tables, then still get into trouble when the analysis
quietly treats two kinds of interviews as though they were the same. Or when a
total and the rate used to build it are based on different trips. Or when a
result is split by a species or section in a way that looks useful but no longer
matches what was actually sampled.

Those are the kinds of problems we have been working through.

## Keeping the estimator with the survey

One of the bigger pieces of work has involved roving interviews. An access
interview happens when an angler has completed a trip. A roving interview
happens while the person is still fishing. The catch and effort in a roving
interview are both partial, and that changes the estimator that makes sense.

It is worth being precise about what that changes. A roving clerk does not only
meet anglers in the middle of a trip. Moving through the fishery, the clerk
intercepts whoever is present, and some of those people happen to be finishing.
What follows from a roving design is that all of those interviews get used
together, complete and incomplete alike, rather than discarding the incomplete
ones. The estimator follows from how the clerk sampled, not from the status of
any one interview. That is also why this had to reach harvest and release.
Harvest and released fish are recorded in the same interception as the catch,
and they are biased the same way.

For a while, different parts of an analysis could make different choices from
the same survey. A catch-rate estimate could follow the roving-survey logic,
while a harvest rate, release rate, or total could quietly follow a different
path. The output looked like a coherent set of results, but the underlying
choices did not always agree.

That work is now in place. When a survey calls for the roving approach, the
catch rate, harvest rate, release rate, and the totals built from them all
follow it. When an analyst wants the older ratio-of-means approach, naming it is
enough to get it. Bus-route and ice designs, which cannot support a
mean-of-ratios total, refuse the argument now instead of accepting it and doing
something else.

That last part is not finished. A sectioned design handed the regression
estimator is still accepted and quietly given ratio-of-means numbers. It is
written down, and it is the next thing of that kind to fix.

That is not a new feature in the usual sense. It is a clearer contract between
the field design and the reported estimate.

## Making sections and species useful

The other major thread is about results that are specific enough to be useful.
Lake-wide estimates matter, but managers often need to know what is happening in
a particular section of a lake or river, or with a particular species.

We have been improving the ways `tidycreel` handles those questions. Species
totals can now be estimated within sections, and the three rate estimators for
catch, harvest, and release are kept in step when a result is grouped by
species. That matters because these functions are closely related. Fixing one
and leaving the other two behind creates estimands that are hard to trust.

There is also a small change that says a lot about how I want the package to
behave. A sectioned result is already one row per section. Asking to group it by
section a second time is not a new analytical question. It is the same split
twice. Previously, that request ended in a message about a duplicated column
name. The message was technically true, but it did not explain the problem in
creel-survey terms.

The revised behavior is simple: stop, explain that the result is already split
by section, and leave the other useful groupings alone. It is a small thing, but
clear errors are part of an analysis workflow. They make it easier to catch a
mistaken request before it becomes a workaround in someone else's script.

## Asking a result how it was made

A creel estimate is a claim about the angler and fish population. That claim is
only checkable if a reader can ask the result how it was made, because the same
survey produces quite different numbers depending on which estimator ran.

On several paths, the result could not answer. A total is effort multiplied by a
rate, so the label it carries names the shape of the calculation rather than the
estimator underneath it. Ratio-of-means, mean-of-ratios, and the truncated
version all came back as the same string. The estimator was chosen, it was used,
and then it had nowhere to land on the way out.

One path was worse than silent. A rate estimated section by section passed the
requested estimator down, computed mean-of-ratios with it, and then labeled the
answer ratio-of-means. On one test design that is 0.87 fish per hour reported
under the name of a method that returns 0.59. Both numbers are defensible. Only
one of them was run. And because a roving survey routes to mean-of-ratios on its
own, nobody had to pass an argument to land there.

Results now record the estimator as the analyst asked for it, on rates,
sectioned rates, and totals. None of the numbers changed. That was the point.
The tests check both sides of the contract: two settings that resolve to the
same calculation must return identical estimates while reporting different
names, while a sectioned result must still differ between methods. A test that
only compared labels could pass even if the code had stopped honoring the
argument.

There is a smaller lesson in how this one was found. The issue we had written
for it described the bug incorrectly. It said a total reported the
mean-of-ratios name. It reports the product-form name, and the label the issue
quoted lives on an intermediate object that gets discarded before an analyst
sees anything, so the repair the issue proposed would not have worked.
Re-deriving the problem from the code before writing any fix is what caught
that, and it turned up two more issues on the way.

## Letting the output describe its inputs

A mean-of-ratios estimate now says which trips it actually used: all trips,
complete trips, or incomplete trips. That matters because the roving-survey
default uses all interviews, while an explicit diagnostic path may use only
incomplete ones. The older banner described every mean-of-ratios result as
though it used incomplete trips, even when it did not.

The update also makes the same diagnostic information available for catch,
harvest, and release rates. Truncation details still appear because they are
part of the estimator. The length-of-stay caution and the pointer to validate
incomplete trips appear only when incomplete trips are actually in the result.
That is a modest change in printed output, but it makes a result more honest
about the data behind it.

## Paying attention to the awkward cases

Some of the most important work is in cases that nobody plans for. A trip
duration is missing. A truncation threshold removes every usable interview. A
warning reports a percentage that is not actually the percentage a reader needs
to judge the problem.

Those are not exciting additions to a package website.

We have been adding checks so that these cases produce an explanation tied to
the survey and the data, rather than an error from somewhere deep in R. A trip
with no recorded duration should be identified as a data issue. A threshold that
leaves no usable trips should say that directly. The point is not to make the
hard decisions disappear. It is to make sure the analyst sees the decision that
needs to be made.

## The larger goal

`tidycreel` is growing around a pretty straightforward idea: a fisheries
estimate should stay connected to the survey that produced it.

That means keeping the calendar, counts, interviews, catch, and biological data
in a workflow that is possible to inspect. It means making the estimator match
the interview design. It means carrying the same decisions through to totals,
species, sections, uncertainty, and reporting. And it means being willing to
stop when a request no longer has a clear statistical meaning.

There will always be more to add. Camera surveys, aerial counts, bus routes, ice
fisheries, connected agency data, and reporting all have their own corners to
work through. For now, the focus is getting the foundation right. The earlier
[introduction to tidycreel](/posts/2026-08-18-introducing-tidycreel.html) and
the post on the [creel design object](/posts/2026-08-27-design-object.html)
provide the broader workflow behind this work.

That is slower than adding features. It is also the part that makes the rest of
the package worth using.

You can follow the package work on
[GitHub](https://github.com/chrischizinski/tidycreel), browse the [reference
site](https://chrischizinski.com/tidycreel/), or read more of the reasoning in
[*Modern Creel Survey Analysis in
R*](https://modern-creel-surveys.netlify.app/).
